newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Rebel Serb leader slams Croat concessions.
newsitem.headline: Rebel Serb leader slams Croat concessions.

text.p: A Serb leader of a rebel enclave in Croatia dismissed as unsatisfactory on Wednesday a human and minority rights package Zagreb offered to smooth the area's return to Croatian rule.

Vojislav Stanimirovic, president of Eastern Slavonia's executive council, told Belgrade-based Tanjug news agency the document contained several positive elements, but "globally does not satisfy" Serb demands.

The United Nations, whose 5,000 peacekeepers monitor the area, praised the package on Monday as "better than had been anticipated". Their mandate in Eastern Slavonia should end on July 15 after minority Serbs take part in a countrywide local election, due in March.

Stanimirovic said the strongest Serb objection was Zagreb's insistence that the region, which the Serbs captured in their 1991 rebellion against Croatia's independence, be divided into two Croatian counties, as envisaged by the constitution.
Instead, the Serbs demand that the entire region, bordering Serbia on the east, remain a single administrative unit.
"That is the most important condition for the Serb population to stay in the area," he said.

About half of some 120,000 Serbs currently living in the region are refugees from other rebel enclaves Zagreb recaptured in 1995. The package gives them the right to choose if they want to vote in Eastern Slavonia or in the areas where they lived before the 1991 war.

Stanimirovic praised parts of the package granting local Serbs educational and cultural autonomy and the right to be exempt from service in the Croatian army for a period of two years after the area was reintegrated into Croatia.
Stanimirovic said the Eastern Slavonia executive council would discuss details of the proposal on Thursday.
He said the U.S. government had been asked to send Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum to the region within the next 10 days to resolve the disputed issue as tensions rose in the area.

He said the perpetrator, armed with a machine gun first destroyed his own flat before killing the woman. A police search was underway, he added.
Croatian radio reported the man was a Serb but Arnold said his ethnicity was not yet established. "This was an individual act committed in an individual town by a deranged individual," he said.
